title: Universe retention
summary: Control-plane upkeep prunes automatically: it runs the same passes in-process (never through the HTTPS relay) when no receipt exists, when the last run ended with rows still eligible, or six hours after the last run started, stops each run after about 60 seconds, and writes a universe_prune_receipts row with rows deleted per table, elapsed time, outcome (drained, budget or failed) and any named refusal. A failed run prints in every project's steering report; Doctor's HC-universe-prune-receipt fails when the last successful receipt is over two days old. After a drained run on PostgreSQL upkeep runs plain VACUUM on the tables it deleted from, so space is reused; files never shrink. One admin command previews or prunes explicit disposable tables using universe settings, bounded committed transactions and permanent reference protections. One apply run continues until a full cycle deletes nothing under one fixed UTC cutoff; a pass that reaches its budget resumes the same table, and a table that reaches its own statement or lock limit is skipped, retried until three limit hits in a row (any deleted batch resets the count) and reported with its reason and recovery. Cohorts lock only their own rows, and events are read as one index range per severity or name window, using concurrent-built (severity, created_at) and (event_name, created_at) indexes; the composite name index also serves name-only lookups. Large backlog completion has disposable-Postgres tests; production proof remains owed. A table left unfinished names its limit (statement or lock timeout). Output is a progress line about every 10 seconds and a short summary; --full and --json keep per-table detail. Existing faster cleanup keeps its original expiry boundaries and cadence; the one-day cutoff only selects remaining old rows and never creates a minimum hold. Source and disposable-database behavior are tested; deployed proof is still owed.
